faq: Do I need a technical background to use this?

No. We write everything in everyday words and explain any technical term the first time it appears. You only need to know who the product is for and what problem it should solve. We help with the rest during the call.
Will you build the product afterwards?
If you want, yes. The scope is written so we or any other developer can quote from it. There is no obligation to build with us, and the document is yours to keep and share.
Can you tell me if my idea will make money?
We cannot predict revenue. We can point out risks, simpler ways to test demand and which features to leave out of version one so you spend less before you learn anything.
What do you need from me before the call?
A few sentences about the idea, who would use it, and any similar products you like or dislike. Sketches or notes are welcome but not required. We send a short question list the day you order.
desc:
SaaS product scoping and feature planning turns a rough idea into a written plan that any developer can price and build. Ecom Swift LLC runs a short call, defines the user and problem, ranks your features and hands you a scope, screen list and build order.

## What is product scoping?

Product scoping is the work of deciding what your software will and will not do before anyone writes code. The output is a document: who the product is for, the problem it solves, a ranked list of features, the screens users will see and the order to build them in.

Think of it as the plan an architect draws before a builder starts. It does not need technical language. It needs to be specific enough that two different developers reading it would build roughly the same thing.

## Why unscoped ideas become expensive

Without a written scope, every conversation with a developer starts from zero, and every developer imagines a different product. Quotes arrive far apart because each one assumes something different. Features get added mid-build, deadlines slip and the budget moves.

Important things also get forgotten: how users sign in, what happens when a payment fails, who manages accounts. They appear late as extra work. A scope brings those questions forward, when answering them costs only a conversation.

## How a clear scope improves the build

A good scope makes comparison fair. When you send the same document to several developers, their quotes describe the same work, so you can judge price, timing and approach side by side. It also protects focus. Sorting features into must have, later and never keeps the first version small enough to finish and learn from.

User stories describe each feature from the customer's point of view, such as "As a coach, I can invite a client and see their progress." They make it easy to check later whether the feature was built correctly. A phased build order means you can launch something useful early and add the rest as evidence arrives.

## What a useful scope document includes

- A plain statement of the problem and who has it.
- A description of the main user types and what each needs.
- A ranked feature list, each marked must have, later or never.
- User stories for the most important features.
- A list of screens, each with a clear name.
- A build order divided into phases.
- A sketch of the data your product stores and the account types it needs.
- Third-party tools it will rely on, and their running costs.
- Risks and open questions, written down so they are not forgotten.
- A short summary you can share with partners, backers or developers.

## How the process works

We start with a call, up to a set length, where you explain the idea and we ask questions. We probe the user, the existing alternatives and the one outcome the product must deliver. After the call we write the scope and send it for your comments.

The Basic package covers the call, a written problem statement and a short list of must-haves. Standard adds a larger ranked list, user stories, a screen list and phases. Premium adds the data outline, tool and cost list, risks and a review call to walk through the document. Competitor comparison and a rough cost range are available as add-ons. We scope; we do not promise that the idea will earn money.

## What to do, and what to avoid

**Do:**
- Describe the problem in one or two sentences before listing features.
- Name a specific first user, not a general audience.
- Be willing to cut features, even ones you love.
- Write down questions you cannot answer yet.
- Keep the document and share it with every developer you speak to.

**Avoid:**
- Treating every feature as equally important.
- Copying a large product's feature list.
- Skipping the account and admin questions.
- Leaving out running costs of third-party tools.
- Starting to build before the must-have list is agreed.

## Who this service is for

Non-technical founders with a strong idea but no technical vocabulary will gain the most. People comparing agency or freelancer quotes who cannot tell why the numbers differ get a fair baseline. Teams whose project keeps growing in the middle of the build can use a scope to stop the drift.

## What we need from you

A few lines on your idea, who you imagine using it, and any examples or competitors you admire. Come with questions and be ready to say no to features. No technical background is needed, and we never ask for passwords or account access for this service.
